messages.subject: NaN from inla.emarginal(...)
parts:
I got NaN from inla.emarginal(..) and I just want to confirm my understanding of how inla.emarginal() works. 
Is it true that inla.emarginal() calculates E[X] by summing over the trapeziums? with the height being x1*f(x1), x2*f(x2) and width being x2-x1, where f(x) is density at x? 
Instead of using inla.emarginal() to calculate E[X], I wrote some code myself, and I got 3.066773e-16, is it possible that if the number is too small, then inla.emarginal() gives NaN? 

Cheers, 
Joyce

On Fri, 2012-07-27 at 04:55 -0700, Joyce Yuan wrote:
> I got NaN from inla.emarginal(..) and I just want to confirm my
> understanding of how inla.emarginal() works.
> Is it true that inla.emarginal() calculates E[X] by summing over the
> trapeziums? with the height being x1*f(x1), x2*f(x2) and width being
> x2-x1, where f(x) is density at x?
> Instead of using inla.emarginal() to calculate E[X], I wrote some code
> myself, and I got 3.066773e-16, is it possible that if the number is
> too small, then inla.emarginal() gives NaN?

Simpson's rule is used for the integration

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simpson%27s_rule

it shouldn't matter if E[X] is small; it do in any case, estimate it by

E[X] / E[1]

to get an ''exact'' normalisation.

if you send me the example that crash, we can fix it.
